q: Large rounded quartzite stones cover the plateau of La Crau, holding the day's heat well into the night. What are they called?
exp: They were rolled smooth by the river and the glaciers long ago. They are famous but not universal: the same appellation also has deep sand and sandstone, which give much lighter, more perfumed wines.

q: A single southern appellation permits thirteen named grapes, eighteen once the colour variants are counted apart. Which appellation?
exp: Grenache, Clairette and Picpoul each exist in more than one colour, which is where the higher figure comes from. Almost nobody plants all of them, and many fine wines use three or four.

q: Warmth, high alcohol, sweet red fruit and a pale rim in a wine from the papal village point to its dominant grape. Which?
exp: It ripens to high sugar and gives little colour, so a young example can look deceptively light for its weight. Old bush vines of it are the backbone of the appellation.

q: One of the classic southern trio needs real heat to ripen and repays it with tannin, colour and a gamey, meaty note. Which grape?
exp: It buds and ripens late, so it only works in the warmest sites. It also brings the ageing capacity that Grenache lacks, which is why so many blends carry a little of it.

q: A guest asks for a rose from the papal village. What do you tell them?
opts: The appellation covers red and white only
Rose there may be made only from Cinsault
Rose there is made but may not be exported
Rose there comes only from the plateau of La Crau
exp: Point them across the river to Tavel or Lirac instead. A grower in the village who makes rose must sell it under a broader appellation.

q: Uniquely strict harvest rules there require picking by hand and what else?
opts: Chaptalisation of any must below the minimum
A single harvest date fixed for the whole appellation
A compulsory sorting of the crop
exp: The sorting must throw out a share of the picking, and the discarded fruit cannot be made into appellation wine at all. Combined with very low permitted yields, it is one of the more demanding sets of rules in France.

q: The minimum alcohol demanded there is the highest of any French appellation. What is it?
exp: In practice most wines land far above it, and fifteen percent is unremarkable. The floor was set to keep out thin wine from over-cropped vines rather than to encourage power.

q: Why does the village carry a papal name at all?
opts: A pope blessed the first vintage of the appellation
The fourteenth-century popes at Avignon kept a castle there
A pope was born in the village
The vineyards belonged to Rome until the Revolution
exp: The popes moved the papacy to Avignon and built a summer residence a few miles north. The ruined keep still stands above the vines and appears on countless labels.

q: Some bottles from the village are moulded with crossed keys beneath a tiara. What does that emblem tell a buyer?
opts: The producer belongs to the local growers' association
The wine comes from a single vineyard
The wine contains all thirteen permitted varieties
The wine was aged at least three years before release
exp: The embossed bottle was adopted in the 1930s as a mark of origin against fraud. It says nothing about the style or the quality of what is inside.

q: Whites are a small part of the village's output. Which description fits them?
opts: Aged oxidatively under a film of yeast
Full-bodied and broad, with modest acidity
exp: Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne and Bourboulenc give weight rather than tension. They are usually drunk young, though the best go quiet for several years and then return.

q: Vineyards climbing to the foot of the jagged limestone teeth of the Dentelles de Montmirail give a Grenache red firmer and fresher than the plain below. Which cru?
exp: Altitude and limestone give cooler nights and better acidity than the valley floor. It is the standard recommendation for a guest who finds Chateauneuf too heavy.

q: Which cru sits immediately south of Gigondas on flatter, stonier ground and makes all three colours?
exp: The two are constantly compared, and the flatter site shows: warmer, rounder and quicker to drink, usually at a friendlier price.

q: A dry rose deep enough in colour to be mistaken for a light red, and the only wine its right-bank appellation may produce. Which appellation?
exp: Colour comes from a longer maceration than a pale Provencal rose gets, and the wine has the structure to take a real main course. It is one of the few roses worth a year or two in bottle.

q: Just north of that rose-only appellation, which right-bank neighbour makes red, white and rose alike?
exp: It shares the same stony terraces and long enjoyed a lesser reputation, largely because Tavel took the attention. Its reds are the argument for looking at the right bank at all.

q: One southern cru is known both for dry red wine and for a fortified sweet wine made from the same grape. Which?
exp: The sweet version comes in pale and dark styles depending on how it is aged, and an oxidative example develops the nutty rancio character. Both are Grenache.

q: A sweet golden wine of grapey, orange-blossom aroma comes from a village beneath the Dentelles de Montmirail. Which appellation?
exp: Made from Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains, the aromatic Muscat rather than the coarser ones. The same village also has its own appellation for dry red wine.
